contact_edits.before: The show may be stale but the production and performances are surprisingly fresh. Jeff Calhoun's direction is smooth, Lisa Stevens' choreography is energetic and Kenneth Foy's sets are excellent -- with their rows and rows of overhead lights, they are impressively spacious and make institutional architecture look like a good idea. John Jeffrey Martin and Arielle Jacobs are an appealing Troy and Gabriella, the only two people in nthe show who resemble real human beings. The rest of the cast don't get that chance, but they caricature with vigour. Chandra Lee Schwartz and Bobby List are as amusing a pair of terrible twins as anyone has a right to expect, given their material, and Ellen Harvey as Ms. Darbus does a very good Carol Burnett; even her passion for the drama is weirdly, indeed alarmingly, believable. Nice too is Olivia Ogama as the timid composer of the show-within-the-show which, for all we are allowed to see or hear of it, may be a masterpiece. (Though, on the basis of the one song we do hear, probably not.) Like everyone else, she gets to pair off at the end; in her case, it's with the school's resident newsreader, who spends the entire show making hysterically cheery announcements and mysteriously gets to the end of the evening without somebody strangling him. I notice that though the casting is proudly multicultural, the actual couplings are strictly intra- racial. And though Ryan, too, is allowed to find a partner, that encounter is kept very coy and upstage. School fiction, in any genre, is always aimed at an audience younger than the characters it depicts -- nobody finds their own contemporaries glamorous --but in this show, the gap yawns wider than ever before. - High School Musical runs until Sept. 23 at the Princess of Wales Theatre. For tickets, call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.com.
